title: King Kanakasuriya Cinkaiariyan
biography: Kanakasuriya Cinkaiariyan ruled Jaffna for 17 years under Kotte's overlordship until Parakramabahu VI's death. He reasserted autonomy after 1467, revitalizing Hindu institutions and trade. His reign marks Jaffna's recovery of independence in the kingdom's twilight.

title: Yongle Emperor (Zhu Di)
biography: Visionary Ming emperor who moved the capital to Beijing, constructed the Forbidden City, rebuilt the Grand Canal, compiled the Yongle Encyclopedia, and sponsored Admiral Zheng He's seven epic maritime treasure voyages.
internationalConnections: Zheng He's treasure fleet established diplomatic ties with Sri Lanka (Kotte), India (Calicut), Hormuz, and East Africa (Malindi).

title: King Karaliyadde Bandara
biography: Karaliyadde Bandara's 29-year reign witnessed increasing Portuguese pressure on Kandy and the rise of Sitawaka. He preserved the Tooth Relic and Buddhist traditions amid regional warfare. Factional intrigue ended his reign, though the kingdom's independence survived.

title: King Dharmasoka
biography: Dharmasoka (1208–1209) ruled for one year within the chaotic late Polonnaruwa succession. His brief tenure limited policy imprints; rapid turnover characterized this volatile period. Administrative survival relied on entrenched local networks.

title: King Khallatanaga
biography: Khallatanaga (Khallata Naga) was briefly mentioned in chronicles as a king during the troubled period after Lanja Tissa. His rule may have been concurrent or contested, reflecting the factional struggles of this era. Details of his reign remain sparse.

title: King Pulahatta
biography: Pulahatta (103–100 BCE) participated in the brief line of usurpers following Valagamba’s early overthrow. Foreign-aligned or opportunistic military backing enabled his rise. His government, lacking enduring cultural or hydraulic markers, is remembered chiefly as part of the interregnum that fractured legitimate dynastic continuity. Removal by Bahiya demonstrates rapid turnover symptomatic of low internal legitimacy.
